title: Where Does Northern B.C. Begin?
summary: Prince George feels northern. Williams Lake often does too. But official maps draw the line in different places, because each boundary was made to answer a different question.
sourceNote: This story uses repository snapshots from the B.C. Ministry of Health, B.C. Energy Regulator, Statistics Canada, and B.C. natural-resource administration. These are administrative and statistical definitions—not a survey of how people describe where they live.
details: Northern B.C. looks obvious until a boundary has to be drawn. Health services, energy regulation, census geography, and natural-resource administration divide the same province for different purposes.

The story is intentionally encoded as data. Its cards declare a camera position, visible layers, and place markers; the reusable story-map workspace turns those declarations into a scrolling map narrative.
Local repository paths can be replaced with HTTPS GeoJSON URLs in another project package, provided the remote host permits browser access.

scenes.label: The question
scenes.title: A line everyone knows—until they try to draw it
scenes.text: Ask where Northern B.C. begins and Prince George is an easy answer. Williams Lake is harder. Rather than choosing one true north, this story compares the boundaries institutions actually use.

scenes.label: Health hierarchy
scenes.title: Health boundaries zoom from province to community
scenes.text: B.C.'s health geography nests four levels: Health Authority, Health Service Delivery Area, Local Health Area, and Community Health Service Area. Turning them on together reveals how a broad service region resolves into local planning units.

scenes.label: Prince George
scenes.title: Prince George is northern in the health system
scenes.text: Prince George sits inside Northern Health. On this map, the everyday description and the service-delivery boundary reinforce each other: the city is clearly on the northern side of the institutional line.

scenes.label: Williams Lake
scenes.title: Williams Lake lands on the other side
scenes.text: Williams Lake sits in Interior Health, close to the boundary with Northern Health. Many regional identities do not stop cleanly at a service boundary, so the health map can feel at odds with how people describe the Cariboo.

scenes.label: Energy
scenes.title: For energy regulation, Prince George is southwest
scenes.text: The B.C. Energy Regulator divides its operating geography into North, Central, South East, and South West zones. Under that administrative map, Prince George sits in South West—a useful reminder that a zone name describes an agency's operating territory, not a universal regional identity.

scenes.label: Census
scenes.title: Statistics Canada draws another north–south line
scenes.text: The North/South variant of the 2021 census classification labels census subdivisions across Canada. Clipped to B.C., it places both Prince George and Williams Lake in the North. This is a statistical classification—not a measure of personal identity—but it produces a boundary closer to many broad regional descriptions.

scenes.label: Resources
scenes.title: Natural-resource administration redraws the province again
scenes.text: Natural Resource Regions organize field operations around areas such as Omineca, Cariboo, Skeena, and the Northeast. These names avoid a single north–south split and instead describe a set of working regions shaped around a different mandate.

scenes.label: What gives?
scenes.title: The boundary is an argument about purpose
scenes.text: None of these maps settles where Northern B.C. truly begins. Each makes a boundary useful for health delivery, regulation, statistics, or resource administration. The better question is not only “Where is north?” but “Who drew this line, and what did they need it to do?”
